planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun. Albemarle is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Albemarle is a self-fertile, black-skinned muscadine named for the Albemarle Sound region of northeastern North Carolina, where it has long been prized as a dependable dooryard and small-vineyard selection. Berries are medium-sized with unusually high sugar content and a dry stem scar that lets fruit be pulled cleanly for fresh eating, juice, or preserves without tearing. It ripens early to midseason and holds up reliably through the humid Carolina and Gulf South growing season. Train vines on a two-wire trellis or arbor and prune hard each winter to keep fruiting wood renewed and productive.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis. Watergate is a female-flowered cultivar and must be planted within range of a self-fertile or male-flowered muscadine for pollination.

directions: Watergate is a bronze-fruited muscadine grown mainly for fresh eating, producing large berries with a good, sweet flavor. The skin runs a bit tougher than some fresh-market bronze selections, which makes the fruit resist splitting and hold well after picking, though individual berries within a cluster tend to color and ripen unevenly rather than all at once. Because it is female-flowered, Watergate needs a nearby self-fertile or male vine to set a crop and is best used as a companion selection alongside a perfect-flowered variety rather than as a stand-alone planting. Site it on a sturdy arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, and pick clusters over several passes as berries finish coloring.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis. Pam is a female-flowered cultivar and needs a nearby self-fertile or male muscadine to pollinate it and produce a crop.

directions: Pam is a heavy-bearing bronze muscadine known for very large, loose clusters that can carry a dozen or more berries, among the biggest cluster counts of the female-flowered bronze varieties. Fruit runs sweet with notably high sugar content and pulls free with a dry stem scar, which helps individual berries keep their shape and quality for several days after harvest. Vines are vigorous, disease-tolerant, and productive once established, making Pam a good choice for a pick-your-own row or a home arbor with plenty of room to spread. Because it bears only female flowers, plant it near a self-fertile variety such as Carlos or Nesbitt to ensure reliable pollination and fruit set.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. Delicious is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Delicious is a self-fertile, black-fruited muscadine bred at the University of Florida from a cross between a bronze parent and a large-fruited self-fertile black selection, released in the late 2000s. The oval berries color to a deep purple-black at full ripeness and the vine ripens its crop earlier than many older black cultivars, making it a useful bridge between early and midseason harvest. Vines are vigorous, disease-resistant, and heavy-bearing, holding up well to the fungal pressure typical of humid Gulf Coast summers. Grow on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, pruning hard each winter to renew fruiting wood.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. Southern Jewel is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Southern Jewel is a self-fertile black to deep-purple muscadine bred at the University of Florida from a cross of the bronze cultivar Granny Val and a large black selection. Its most distinctive trait is fruiting habit: berries form in tight bunches of roughly six to twelve that cling firmly to the stem rather than dropping individually, so whole clusters can be picked and handled like bunch grapes instead of gathering loose berries off the ground. The thin, tender skin and crisp, crunchy flesh make it especially well suited to fresh eating, with good disease resistance and heavy yields under humid Southern conditions. Grow on a sturdy arbor or trellis in full sun, and expect this warm-climate selection to perform best in the Gulf Coast and peninsular Florida heat it was bred for.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. Gold Delight has hermaphroditic (perfect) flowers and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Gold Delight is a recent University of Georgia release, selected from a cross of Early Fry and Tara, that combines self-fertility with unusually large bronze berries for an early-to-midseason cultivar. In UGA trials it showed better resistance to fruit rot than older bronze standards and lost less moisture in cold storage, giving it noticeably better shelf life than many bronze muscadines sold fresh. The vigorous, self-fertile vines need no separate pollinator and bear heavily once established, making this a strong choice where growers want the large-berried, high-sugar eating quality of Fry-type muscadines with improved rot tolerance in humid weather. Train on a sturdy arbor or two-wire trellis in full sun and well-drained soil.

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container vines in spring on a sturdy trellis in full sun. RazzMatazz is self-fertile (perfect-flowered) and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: RazzMatazz is a patented hybrid between muscadine grape and European wine/table grape (Vitis vinifera), bred to combine muscadine-type disease resistance with the seedless berries and thin skin of a bunch grape. Fruit is deep red with crisp flesh and a sweet flavor, and unlike most muscadines the self-fertile vines flower and ripen berries continuously from midsummer until frost rather than in a single concentrated harvest window. It ripens earlier than most straight muscadine cultivars and has shown strong resistance to the fungal diseases that trouble bunch grapes in humid Southern climates, allowing it to be grown with minimal spraying. Train on a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun and well-drained soil, and expect a more compact, less sprawling vine than typical full-size muscadine cultivars.
